strengths: Well-motivated problem: inducing few-shot capabilities in smaller (<7B) LMMs where ICL is known to be unreliable (Zong et al., 2025), with a clear hypothesis (image-embedding overload) that the method and experiments are designed around.

Technically sound method description: MAPD combines first-order MAML (FoMAML with learnable per-step inner learning rates) with prompt distillation via an attention-mapper, and the formulation (inner/outer loop, Eq. 2–5, Algorithm 1) is clearly specified and easy to follow.

Strong, fair baseline design within the shared architecture: Multi-TaskPD, In-ContextPD, Model-AvgPD, and NoMeta-taskPD isolate the contributions of meta-tasks and bi-level optimization; comparisons across both ICL and FT test-time adaptation are informative.

Ablations go beyond headline numbers: effect of soft-prompt length vs. shots, decomposition of Operator Induction into Task Induction / Perception / Math Reasoning, few-shot example selection (Same Attribute / Same Pair), and perturbation robustness (Table 2).

Good reproducibility practices: detailed data mixture (802K examples), hyperparameters, training compute, test-time adaptation protocol (K selection via validation), released code, LLM-as-judge prompts, and qualitative examples.
Honest limitations section: acknowledges single-image scope, substantially higher test-time compute (5x ICL, quantified in TFLOPs), and that MAPD requires FT-based adaptation.
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: the attention-mapper is explicitly 'inspired from Najdenkoska et al. (2023)' and the meta-learning component is a standard FoMAML application; the contribution is primarily a combination of known techniques applied at LMM scale rather than a new algorithmic idea.

Narrow evaluation scope: only four single-image tasks from a single benchmark (VL-ICL Bench), two of which have very small query sets (Operator Induction: 60 queries), raising concerns about statistical significance of the reported margins; no error bars or significance tests are reported.

Gains over the strongest baselines are modest and inconsistent: MAPD beats Multi-TaskPD by only ~1.5% on CLEVR and ~3.5% on TextOCR, and underperforms In-ContextPD under ICL adaptation on three tasks; the headline claim of 'consistently outperforming' rests mainly on the FT setting.

Missing key test-time adaptation baselines: there is no comparison to test-time prompt tuning (e.g., TPT), entropy-minimization TTA methods (TENT/MEMO), or test-time LoRA/PEFT fine-tuning of the same architecture, which would establish whether the MAML meta-training is actually necessary versus simple test-time fine-tuning of cheap adapters.

The LLM substitution (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct in place of Vicuna) plus new vision-language data confounds comparisons with published LLaVA models in Table 9, and the model still trails LLaVA-OneVision-72B on three of four tasks.

Evaluation protocol concerns: test-time hyperparameters (K up to 30 steps, learning rate selected per method from a validation set) introduce potential selection bias favoring FT adaptation over training-free ICL, and the math-reasoning subtask relies on a Qwen-2.5-VL-32B judge of the same model family, risking self-preference bias.
0-shot column is left uninterpreted ('We do not compare on 0-shot results') even though several methods show non-trivial 0-shot numbers, leaving an unexplained gap in the analysis.

strengths: The paper is clearly written, with a well-motivated problem setting (inconsistent ICL in smaller LMMs) and a clean formalization of the few-shot VQA meta-learning problem.

The experimental comparison is thorough relative to its own framework: MAPD is compared against several sensible alternatives (Multi-Task, In-Context, Model-Avg, NoMeta-task distillation) under both ICL and test-time finetuning adaptation.

Good ablation coverage: scaling with number of soft prompts, few-shot example selection by similarity, robustness to image perturbations, and a decomposition of the Operator Induction task into perception/task induction/reasoning.
Reproducibility is above average: code release promised, full data mixture, hyperparameters, learning rates, training times, and test-time adaptation procedure are all documented in the appendix.
The approach is parameter-efficient (24M trainable parameters) and the monotonic improvement with number of shots is a genuinely desirable property that standard ICL lacks.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method is a fairly straightforward combination of well-known components — first-order MAML (Finn et al., 2017 / Antoniou et al., 2019), prompt tuning (Lester et al., 2021), and an attention-based projector that the authors themselves state is 'inspired from' Najdenkoska et al. (2023). The core architectural and algorithmic machinery is borrowed; the contribution is primarily an application/instantiation at LMM scale.

The central hypothesis — that ICL fails in smaller LMMs because image embeddings contain task-irrelevant information that overwhelms the model — is never directly tested. There is no analysis showing the distilled prompts actually remove task-irrelevant information or explaining *why* meta-learning helps; the hypothesis is invoked to motivate the method but not validated.

Evaluation scope is narrow: only four single-image tasks from a single benchmark (VL-ICL Bench). Open-MI is a 2-way classification task (~50% chance baseline), which inflates averages; absolute performance on CLEVR (~31%) and TextOCR (~26%) is quite low, so the practical significance of the gains is questionable.

The margin of MAPD over the much simpler Multi-Task baseline is small and inconsistent across tasks (e.g., 31.4 vs 29.9 on CLEVR, 26.4 vs 22.9 on TextOCR, and MAPD's ICL adaptation is actually worse than baselines on several tasks). No error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed results are reported — with only 60 query examples for Operator Induction, these differences may not be statistically meaningful.

Confounded comparisons: the proposed model also swaps in a stronger backbone (Qwen2.5-7B) and replaces the MLP projector with an attention-mapper, so it is unclear how much of the improvement over LLaVA baselines comes from meta-learning versus the architecture/backbone changes. The claimed advantage over Multi-TaskPD (same architecture) is where the meta-learning contribution must stand, and that margin is thin.

The 'few-shot adaptation' framing is weakened by the test-time procedure: 30 gradient steps of finetuning per task plus validation-based checkpoint/learning-rate selection (10% of training data reserved for validation, best K selected by validation loss), which partly contradicts the low-data claim and increases test-time compute ~5x over ICL (as the authors acknowledge in A.4).

External competitiveness is limited: in Table 9, LLaVA-OneVision-72B with plain ICL still substantially outperforms MAPD on 3 of 4 tasks (e.g., 69.1 vs 47.7 on Operator Induction, 52.2 vs 26.4 on TextOCR), and much of the headline 'beats ICL' result is simply that finetuning beats in-context prompting (even NoMeta-task FT is competitive).

Some results undermine the narrative of consistent superiority: MAPD under ICL adaptation (9.6 avg on Operator Induction, 7.3 on TextOCR) is among the worst methods, and 0-shot behavior is excluded from comparison without full justification.

Broader significance is unclear: the method targets small LMMs where ICL is weak, but the fixed soft-prompt bottleneck (m=256 tokens) and the requirement for per-task gradient adaptation may not scale to richer multi-image or long-context settings, which the authors defer to future work.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: the paper targets the well-documented failure of ICL in smaller (<7B) LMMs (Zong et al., 2025) and proposes a principled meta-learning alternative rather than just scaling context length.

Technically sound and clearly described method: the FoMAML-based bi-level optimization over an attention-mapper + soft prompts is cleanly formulated (Eqs. 2-5, Algorithm 1), parameter-efficient (~24M trainable params), and the ablations cover the key design choices (number of prompts, shots, meta-task curation).

Thorough and largely fair evaluation: multiple prompt-distillation baselines (Multi-TaskPD, In-ContextPD, Model-AvgPD, NoMeta-taskPD) are implemented on the *same* architecture and LLM, which properly isolates the contribution of meta-learning from the stronger Qwen2.5 backbone; additional analyses (perturbation robustness, similarity-based few-shot selection, subtask breakdown, scaling to 64 shots, comparison against LLaVA-OneVision models) add depth.

Good reproducibility: detailed data mixture, hyperparameters, training times, compute, test-time adaptation protocol, and a code release are all provided; limitations (single-image only, 5x test-time compute of FT vs ICL) are honestly acknowledged.
The few-shot selection and perturbation analyses are informative beyond the main claim and suggest the meta-learned initialization is genuinely more robust rather than just more accurate.
weaknesses: Limited novelty in composition: the method is essentially FoMAML + prompt tuning + an attention-mapper adopted from Najdenkoska et al. (2023), applied to LLaVA; each ingredient is established and the In-ContextPD/MetaICL-style alternative already exists in the literature. The contribution is a careful integration rather than a new technique.

Narrow evaluation scope: all main results come from only four single-image tasks of VL-ICL Bench; no standard LMM benchmarks (e.g., VQAv2, MMBench, MathVista held-out splits) are reported, so it is unclear whether the attention-mapper + prompt distillation pipeline regresses on general VQA capability that the original LLaVA v1.5 provides.

Statistical rigor is missing: no seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests; several wins are small (e.g., CLEVR 31.4 vs 29.9, TextOCR 26.4 vs 22.9) and MAPD actually *loses* to simpler baselines in some cells (e.g., MAPD with ICL adaptation on Operator Induction, 9.6 vs 12.1), weakening the 'consistently outperforms' claim, which really holds only for the FT-based setting.

The FT-vs-ICL comparison is somewhat asymmetric: FT adaptation uses 30 gradient steps per shot plus validation-based selection of K and learning rate (using 10% of the test task's training split), while ICL gets no such tuning budget; the headline 21.2% improvement partly conflates 'prompt distillation' with 'test-time gradient access', and FT costs ~5x the compute of ICL, which limits practical significance.

The central 'distillation' framing is loose: the soft prompts are learnable parameters fused with image embeddings via attention, not a distillation of task-specific information in a precise sense; the causal claim that ICL fails because models are 'overwhelmed by image embedding information' is plausible but not directly tested.

Presentation issues: footnote 1 (code link) is incomplete; minor typos ('Stricly', 'capabilties'); the 0-shot column is trivially uninformative (the adapted model has no learned prompts), so claims of 'strictly monotonic improvements' start from a degenerate baseline.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and well-documented problem (non-monotonic/erratic ICL behavior in smaller LMMs) with a clear hypothesis supported by a motivating experiment (I2T vs. T2T comparison in Figure 2), which is a nice empirical contribution in itself.

The proposed MAPD method is technically coherent: first-order MAML over a jointly trained attention-mapper + soft prompt projection layer is a sensible and parameter-efficient design (24M trainable params), and the two-stage curriculum follows established LLaVA practice.

Evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: four VL-ICL tasks, five prompt-distillation baselines (including well-motivated ablations like In-ContextPD and Multi-TaskPD), LoRA comparisons at matched parameter counts, four LMM architecture variants, robustness to image perturbations, few-shot selection strategies, shot scaling to 64, attention entropy analysis, and a FLOPs-matched compute comparison against ICL.

Key claims are supported: MAPD with few-step finetuning beats ICL by ~21.2% on average and beats the best LoRA configuration by ~7.7%, and is the only method showing strictly monotonic improvements with more shots.

The appendix provides substantial reproducibility detail: exact data mixtures, meta-task compositions, grid-searched hyperparameters, learning-rate tables, and qualitative prediction trajectories over gradient steps; code release is promised.
The compute analysis (Section A.3) honestly reports FT's latency disadvantage and frames the tradeoff fairly rather than hiding it.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental. The core components are all well established: FoMAML (Finn et al., 2017; Antoniou et al., 2019), prompt tuning (Lester et al., 2021), meta-learned soft prompts bridging vision and language models (Najdenkoska et al., 2023, which the paper itself acknowledges and extends mainly by using patch features instead of a CLS token), and in-context tuning (Chen et al., 2022; Min et al., 2022). The claim of 'first exploration of meta-learned prompt distillation for cross-task generalization in LMMs' is a narrow novelty claim resting mostly on the LMM setting.

The headline evaluation scope is narrow: only four single-image tasks from a single benchmark (VL-ICL Bench), all of which are highly stylized (nonsense names, synthetic operator induction, synthetic counting, OCR). There is no evaluation on more naturalistic few-shot VQA tasks, which weakens the generality of the conclusions; multi-image settings are deferred to future work.

MAPD is not uniformly superior: under ICL adaptation it performs poorly on Operator Induction (9.6) and CLEVR (12.3), well below In-ContextPD (20.6 and 24.1) and even NoMeta-taskPD on OP_IND; and In-ContextPD matches or beats it on some tasks/settings. This complicates the 'meta-learning is best' narrative and deserves more analysis of when meta-learning helps vs. hurts.

The central hypothesis (LMMs are 'overwhelmed' by extraneous information in image embeddings) is supported only indirectly (I2T vs T2T gap, FT improvements on public LMMs) and is not validated mechanistically beyond a coarse attention-entropy analysis; the causal story remains somewhat speculative.

Practical significance is limited: per-query latency roughly doubles vs. ICL, gradient-based test-time adaptation on every query is operationally awkward, and the reported accuracy on some tasks (TextOCR ~26%, CLEVR ~31%) remains low in absolute terms. Compared to simply using a stronger public model (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL-7B with FT reaches 85.6 on Open-MI vs. MAPD's 77.9), the end-to-end value proposition is not fully established.

Some experimental asymmetries: hyperparameters (context length, meta-task compositions) differ across methods, model selection uses a validation set drawn from the same task distribution, and direct comparisons to public LMMs are not apples-to-apples (acknowledged, but the Table 13 narrative still leans on these comparisons).

Writing has minor issues (e.g., undefined 'Table' reference in A.1.2, typos such as 'Stricly', 'optmization', 'given' instead of 'give' in prompts, inconsistent shot notation), and the empty code-release footnote weakens reproducibility claims at submission time.

strengths: The paper is empirically thorough: it evaluates on a recognized benchmark (VL-ICL), includes multiple well-motivated baselines (Multi-TaskPD, In-ContextPD, Model-AvgPD, NoMeta-taskPD, several LoRA configurations), and reports results across shots, architectures (different LLMs and vision encoders), with confidence intervals and reproducibility details (grid searches, learning rates, training times).

The ablation studies are informative: the projection-layer comparison (Figure 5), soft-prompt length analysis (Figure 4a), attention-entropy analysis (A.2.10), robustness to image perturbations (A.2.7), few-shot selection strategies (A.2.8), and FLOPs-matched compute comparison (A.3) go beyond what many submissions provide.

The empirical observation motivating the work (I2T ICL degrading with more image tokens while T2T improves, Figure 2) is interesting and well presented, and the idea of distilling image information into a fixed, test-time-adaptable set of soft prompts is a reasonable solution with practical appeal (bounded context length, monotonic scaling with shots).
The method is parameter-efficient (24M trainable parameters) and the test-time adaptation converges within ~30 gradient steps, which is practically attractive for low-data adaptation scenarios.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method is a fairly direct combination of well-known components — first-order MAML (Finn et al., 2017; Antoniou et al., 2019), prompt tuning (Lester et al., 2021), and an attention-mapper adapted from Najdenkoska et al. (2023) (the paper itself admits it is 'inspired by' and merely replaces the CLS token with all patch features). The framing of 'first exploration of meta-learned prompt distillation for cross-task generalization in LMMs' is a thin delta over existing work (MetaICL, in-context tuning, meta-prompt learning for VL models).

The headline claims are somewhat misleading. The claimed '21.2% over ICL' largely reflects a comparison between gradient-based fine-tuning and pure ICL, which is known to favor FT (and is confirmed in the paper's own Table 13, where FT improves every public LMM). The more meaningful meta-learning claim is the 7.7% over the best LoRA configuration, which is a modest gain.

Weak absolute performance and questionable practical significance: in Table 13, the proposed LAQ-7B+MAPD substantially underperforms even 7B public models (LLaVA-OneVision-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B) on 3 of 4 tasks (e.g., 47.7 vs 84.2/89.4 on OP_IND; 26.4 vs 42.3/50.5 on TextOCR), only winning on Open-MI. It is unclear what a practitioner gains by adopting this pipeline over simply using a stronger pretrained LMM.

Internal inconsistencies in the results undermine the story: with ICL adaptation, MAPD performs worst among meta-task methods on 3 of 4 tasks (e.g., 9.6 on OP_IND, below even the non-meta NoMeta-taskPD at 12.1), which is hard to reconcile with the claim that MAPD meta-learns the best prompt initialization. The paper does not adequately explain this asymmetry between ICL and FT adaptation.

Narrow evaluation scope: only 4 single-image tasks from VL-ICL are used, three of which (Open-MI, CLEVR, Operator Induction) are synthetic/nonsense-label tasks; generalization to natural VQA distributions and the multi-image setting is deferred to future work, making the 'various VQA tasks' claim in the abstract stronger than the evidence.

Evaluation protocol concerns: the test-time adaptation hyperparameters (learning rates in Table 10, K=30 steps) are selected using a validation set sampled from the same test-task training splits, and model selection is done per task — this blurs the line between task adaptation and task-specific tuning, which is precisely the distinction the paper is trying to draw against ICL.

The claim that MAPD 'can be applied to any LMM architecture' is only partially supported: the cross-architecture experiments (Table 3) vary components of the authors' own LLaVA-style model, and the paper concedes (A.2.5) that attention-mapper finetuning on stronger public LMMs (LLaVA-OneVision, Qwen-VL) was infeasible, so the generalization claim is untested on the most relevant models.

Presentation issues: several typos ('Stricly', 'optmization', truncated equations in Section 3.1 and Eq. 9 formatting, stray comma in Section 4.3), and the abstraction/conclusion oversell the scope of the contribution relative to the experimental evidence.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: the paper builds a convincing empirical case (Figure 2, I2T vs T2T gap; Figure 1 failure case) that image embeddings in long contexts impair ICL in smaller LMMs, and connects this to a concrete solution (distilling task-relevant visual features into fixed soft prompts).

The proposed method (MAPD) is technically coherent: a flexible attention-mapper projection layer jointly trained with soft prompts using first-order MAML over meta-tasks, with the practical benefit of only ~24M trainable parameters and few gradient steps (K ≤ 30) at test time.

Extensive and mostly well-designed evaluation: the paper compares against carefully constructed ablation-style baselines (Multi-TaskPD, In-ContextPD, NoMeta-taskPD, Model-AvgPD), LoRA configurations matched by parameter count, and multiple LMM/vision-encoder configurations (Table 3), which supports the claim that meta-learning specifically (not just prompt distillation) drives the gains.

Rich analysis beyond headline numbers: ablations on projection-layer designs (Figure 5), soft prompt count scaling (Figure 4a), attention-entropy analysis (Table 15), robustness to image perturbations (Table 14), few-shot selection strategies, subtask decomposition of Operator Induction, and an honest test-time compute/latency analysis (Appendix A.3) that acknowledges FT is ~2x slower than ICL but scales better with compute.

Reproducibility: hyperparameter grids, meta-task composition tables, training times, and code release are provided; test-time protocols follow the established VL-ICL benchmark construction, and the paper honestly scopes its claims to single-image tasks.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method is a combination of well-known components — first-order MAML/FoMAML, prompt tuning, and an attention-based projector closely inspired by Najdenkoska et al. (2023). The main delta over prior meta-learned prompt work is applying it to LMMs and using full patch features rather than a CLS token. This is an empirical contribution more than a conceptual one.

Evaluation scope is narrow: only four single-image tasks from VL-ICL Bench are used, with small test sets (e.g., Operator Induction has only 60 query examples; results in Table 11 lack confidence intervals on some tables), making some of the reported differences (e.g., MAPD vs Multi-TaskPD of 1-3 points) less statistically compelling. The 'first exploration' and 'SOTA' framing overstates what 4 tasks can support.

Cross-model comparisons are partially apples-to-oranges: the strongest results come from a custom base model (LLaVA-ATT-Qwen2.5-7B) trained on 1.3M examples, whereas public LMMs (LLaVA-OneVision-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B) with FT actually outperform MAPD on most tasks except Open-MI (Table 13). The paper acknowledges this, but the headline comparisons could mislead readers about the practical advantage of MAPD over simply fine-tuning a stronger existing LMM.

Inconsistent behavior of the method under ICL adaptation: MAPD is notably worse than baselines under ICL on Operator Induction (9.6 avg, worse than NoMeta-taskPD's 12.1) and CLEVR/TextOCR, meaning the benefits are contingent on test-time gradient steps — a practical cost the paper only partially mitigates in the compute analysis.

Hyperparameter and protocol dependence: test-time adaptation requires selecting the best K-step checkpoint via a validation loss over a held-out slice of the training split and per-task learning-rate selection (grid over [0.1, 1.0]); this adds test-time machinery whose sensitivity is not fully ablated, and the very high test-time learning rates (up to 1.0) raise questions about stability across unseen tasks.

Some claims lack direct evidence: e.g., the hypothesis that LMMs are 'overwhelmed by extraneous information' is supported only indirectly via performance gaps and attention entropy; no mechanistic analysis of what the distilled soft prompts encode (beyond attention statistics) is provided.
